summary: Describes a SIP extension providing a general framework for nodes to request notification from remote nodes when certain events occur. It was replaced by RFC 6665.

plainLanguage.summary: It is like subscribing to a message that says tell me when something changes. It has been replaced by RFC 6665.

questions: what is sip subscribe and notify
how does sip event notification work
what is a sip event package
subtitle: A SIP framework for asking another node to tell you when something changes, using SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY.

tldr.problem: SIP services such as buddy lists, message waiting indications and automatic callback need one node to learn when the state of something on another node changes.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3265 adds the SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY methods plus the Event, Allow-Events and Subscription-State headers. A subscriber asks a notifier for a resource's state, and the notifier sends NOTIFY requests as the state changes.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is only a base framework that must be extended by event packages, and it has since been obsoleted by RFC 6665.

facts.label: Event rate warning
facts.value: More than about once per second is excessive

today: RFC 3265 has been obsoleted by RFC 6665, which is the document to follow now. It was also updated by RFC 5367, RFC 5727 and RFC 6446.

sections.title: A Framework for Event Notification
sections.content:
Many SIP services need asynchronous notification of events. The RFC names automatic callback (based on terminal state), buddy lists (based on user presence), message waiting indications (based on mailbox state) and PSTN and Internet Internetworking (PINT) status (based on call state).

This document does not describe an extension that can be used directly. It is an abstract base class, in the RFC's own object-oriented analogy, which other documents called event packages must extend. It also states plainly that it is not meant to be a general-purpose infrastructure for all kinds of event subscription and notification. The goal is a SIP-specific framework that is simple enough for simple features and flexible enough for powerful services.
sections.plainLanguage: This note is the blueprint for a 'tell me when it changes' service. You still need a separate note for each kind of thing you want to be told about.

sections.title: Subscribers, Notifiers and Subscriptions
sections.content:
A subscriber is a user agent that receives NOTIFY requests about the state of a resource. A notifier is a user agent that generates those NOTIFY requests, and it normally also accepts SUBSCRIBE requests. A subscription is a set of application state tied to a SIP dialog, including the event package name and possibly an identification token. It exists in both the subscriber and the notifier.

A state agent is a notifier that publishes state on behalf of a resource and may gather it from several sources. Subscription migration means moving a subscription from one notifier to another.

Which event is meant is identified by three things: the Request URI, the Event header type, and optionally a message body. A subscriber MUST include exactly one Event header in a SUBSCRIBE. Its token is registered with IANA and corresponds to an event package. An optional id parameter tells apart several subscriptions inside one dialog.
sections.plainLanguage: The person asking is the subscriber, the person who tells is the notifier, and the deal between them is the subscription.

sections.title: SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY Behavior
sections.content:
A subscriber sends SUBSCRIBE, which SHOULD carry an Expires header giving the subscription duration. A 200-class response MUST also contain Expires. The notifier may shorten the time but MUST NOT lengthen it. To keep the subscription going the subscriber refreshes it with a new SUBSCRIBE on the same dialog, and a SUBSCRIBE with Expires of 0 unsubscribes. The notifier MUST NOT wait for a user decision before giving a final response. If it cannot decide at once, or wants to hide its policy, it returns 202 Accepted, and an unknown event package gets 489 Bad Event.

After accepting or refreshing a subscription, the notifier MUST immediately send a NOTIFY with the current state, even if authorization is still pending. Later it SHOULD send a NOTIFY whenever the state changes, subject to authorization, policy and throttling. One SUBSCRIBE can therefore lead to several NOTIFY requests. Each NOTIFY MUST have a Subscription-State header with the value active, pending or terminated. A terminated state can carry a reason telling the subscriber whether to retry.

Other points: a NOTIFY for an unknown subscription MUST get a 481 response, and a notifier that receives 481 MUST remove the subscription. If a NOTIFY times out and the subscription was installed by a soft-state mechanism such as SUBSCRIBE, the notifier SHOULD remove it. A SUBSCRIBE with Expires of 0 also gives a one-off fetch of state, but polling should be used sparingly. Because requests can fork, a subscriber MUST be ready to receive NOTIFY requests from several dialogs and even before the SUBSCRIBE transaction completes.
sections.plainLanguage: You ask to be told about something for a while. Each time it changes you get a message, and when the time runs out you must ask again if you still care.

sections.title: Event Packages
sections.content:
The framework leaves the details of any particular kind of event to an event package. A package defines the set of state information a notifier reports and any extra syntax needed to carry it. A package MUST give its event token name, define body types for SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY, set a default Expires value, and describe how the notifier handles SUBSCRIBE and generates NOTIFY. It also MUST say whether forked SUBSCRIBE requests may install multiple subscriptions. Behavior marked SHOULD or MUST in this RFC cannot be weakened by a package.

The RFC advises designers to ask whether SIP is really the right tool, and it warns against events that occur more often than about once per second. Packages should send complete state rather than bare events so subscribers do not have to track state themselves. For small state (on the order of 1 kb) it suggests sending the complete state. For large state, a package may send deltas with a version number that increases by exactly one for each NOTIFY. If a subscriber sees a gap, it sends a new SUBSCRIBE to get a full snapshot.

Event template-packages are a special kind that apply to any other package. A template named winfo applied to presence becomes the token presence.winfo, which is why registered tokens MUST NOT contain a dot. The RFC itself registers no packages.
sections.plainLanguage: The big rulebook says how to ask and answer. Each kind of news, like who is online, needs its own small rulebook too.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Subscriptions can reveal private information, so the notifier's user should control who may subscribe, and the notifier should be able to reject subscribers by identity. To avoid revealing policy, a notifier SHOULD return a 202 response and then send a NOTIFY that looks like it could be valid data, even if it is not the true state.

The RFC lists several threats. One SUBSCRIBE that triggers a response and one or more NOTIFY requests can be used as an amplifier in a smurf attack, and subscription state can be used to use up a victim's resources, so notifiers SHOULD require authentication. Replayed SUBSCRIBE or NOTIFY messages can install old subscriptions or spoof old state, so implementations SHOULD use authentication with anti-replay protection. Man-in-the-middle attackers could install, hijack or terminate subscriptions, so integrity protection SHOULD cover key headers and bodies. Implementations MAY encrypt state and SHOULD be able to handle encrypted SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY messages. The mechanisms themselves are those of SIP.
sections.plainLanguage: Not everyone should be allowed to ask what you are up to, and messages must be checked so nobody can fake them or replay old ones.

viz.caption: TYPICAL SUBSCRIBE AND NOTIFY FLOW (RFC 3265, SECTION 1.1)
REASONS GIVEN WHEN SUBSCRIPTION-STATE IS TERMINATED

items.label: Retry now
items.desc: Subscription ended, but the subscriber SHOULD retry immediately with a new one. Used to migrate subscriptions.

items.label: Retry later
items.desc: Subscription ended; the client SHOULD retry later, waiting at least retry-after seconds if given.

items.label: Do not retry
items.desc: Ended because of a change in authorization policy. Clients SHOULD NOT re-subscribe.

items.label: Not refreshed
items.desc: Ended because it was not refreshed before it expired. Clients MAY re-subscribe immediately.

items.label: No authorization
items.desc: Notifier could not obtain authorization in time. The client may retry, perhaps after retry-after seconds.

items.label: Resource gone
items.desc: The monitored resource no longer exists. Clients SHOULD NOT re-subscribe.
